1	// Package tokens defines the post-protocol token shape and helpers for
2	// reading unverified claims out of JWT access tokens.
3	//
4	// The wire-shape responses from RFC 8628 / RFC 8693 endpoints are
5	// translated into a single TokenSet with absolute expiry. Clients that
6	// only ever see access tokens as opaque bearer strings need not import
7	// this package directly.
8	package tokens
9	
10	import (
11		"encoding/base64"
12		"encoding/json"
13		"errors"
14		"fmt"
15		"strings"
16		"time"
17	)
18	
19	// TokenSet is an OAuth token bundle returned from a device-flow or
20	// token-exchange endpoint, normalised to absolute expiry.
21	//
22	// RefreshToken is empty when the issuer didn't return one. ExpiresAt is
23	// zero for tokens that don't carry a wire-side expires_in.
24	type TokenSet struct {
25		AccessToken  string
26		RefreshToken string
27		TokenType    string
28		ExpiresAt    time.Time
29		Scope        string
30	}
31	
32	// HasRefresh reports whether the set carries a refresh token.
33	func (t TokenSet) HasRefresh() bool { return t.RefreshToken != "" }
34	
35	// String redacts the AccessToken and RefreshToken so accidental
36	// log/print-debug exposure (e.g. `fmt.Printf("%+v", ts)`) doesn't
37	// leak the bearer to the user's terminal, log aggregator, or crash
38	// report. Length of the elided value is preserved so callers can
39	// still tell "had a token / didn't" at a glance.
40	//
41	// To get the raw values, read the struct fields directly. Note that
42	// fmt and log packages reach for Stringer first, so the redacted
43	// form is what shows up by default.
44	func (t TokenSet) String() string {
45		expiresAt := "zero"
46		if !t.ExpiresAt.IsZero() {
47			expiresAt = t.ExpiresAt.Format(time.RFC3339)
48		}
49		return fmt.Sprintf(
50			"TokenSet{AccessToken:%s RefreshToken:%s TokenType:%q ExpiresAt:%s Scope:%q}",
51			ElideSecret(t.AccessToken),
52			ElideSecret(t.RefreshToken),
53			t.TokenType,
54			expiresAt,
55			t.Scope,
56		)
57	}
58	
59	// GoString delegates to String so %#v in fmt also redacts the secret
60	// fields. Without this, `fmt.Sprintf("%#v", ts)` would dump the raw
61	// struct and reveal the AccessToken.
62	func (t TokenSet) GoString() string { return t.String() }
63	
64	// ElideSecret returns a `<elided:N bytes>` placeholder when s is
65	// non-empty, `""` otherwise. Length is preserved so callers can see
66	// "this had a token of length N" without seeing the token itself.
67	// Exported because deviceflow.DeviceCode and sts.ExchangeRequest
68	// both have their own Stringer methods that need to redact secrets
69	// in the same way — duplicating this two-line helper across three
70	// packages would invite the same fix-one-miss-the-other hazard as
71	// the sanitize duplication v0.2.0 consolidated.
72	func ElideSecret(s string) string {
73		if s == "" {
74			return `""`
75		}
76		return fmt.Sprintf("<elided:%d bytes>", len(s))
77	}
78	
79	// Expired reports whether the access token's advertised lifetime has
80	// elapsed at now. Returns false for tokens with a zero ExpiresAt.
81	func (t TokenSet) Expired(now time.Time) bool {
82		if t.ExpiresAt.IsZero() {
83			return false
84		}
85		return !now.Before(t.ExpiresAt)
86	}
87	
88	// ShouldRefresh reports whether the access token is within skew of
89	// expiring (or has already expired). Tokens without an advertised
90	// expiry never need refreshing.
91	func (t TokenSet) ShouldRefresh(now time.Time, skew time.Duration) bool {
92		if t.ExpiresAt.IsZero() {
93			return false
94		}
95		return !now.Add(skew).Before(t.ExpiresAt)
96	}
97	
98	// UnverifiedClaims holds the fields parsed from a JWT access token's
99	// payload. The name carries a deliberate warning: the signature is
100	// not verified by this library, so the fields are attacker-controlled
101	// if an unsigned JWT slips through.
102	//
103	// Signature verification is the issuing server's responsibility; this
104	// package never validates signatures. Clients read claims for routing
105	// (which issuer, which audience) and UX (display the principal
106	// handle) — never as a security boundary.
107	type UnverifiedClaims struct {
108		Issuer    string
109		Subject   string
110		Audience  []string
111		Handle    string
112		ExpiresAt time.Time
113		IssuedAt  time.Time
114		NotBefore time.Time
115	}
116	
117	// ErrMalformedJWT is returned by ParseClaims when the input is not a
118	// well-formed JWT (three base64url-encoded segments separated by dots).
119	var ErrMalformedJWT = errors.New("malformed JWT")
120	
121	// ErrUnsignedJWT is returned by ParseClaims when the JWT header
122	// declares `alg: none`. The unsigned-JWT shape was deprecated by
123	// RFC 7518 §3.6 and is a known attack vector (an attacker can craft
124	// arbitrary claims that pass shape checks). Defense in depth: even
125	// though this package never trusts claims for authorization
126	// decisions, we refuse to parse them so a future caller can't be
127	// tricked into routing on attacker-controlled values.
128	var ErrUnsignedJWT = errors.New("refusing to parse unsigned JWT (alg:none)")
129	
130	// ParseClaims decodes the payload segment of jwt without verifying the
131	// signature. Audience is normalised to a slice even when the wire form
132	// is a single string.
133	//
134	// Rejects JWTs whose header declares `alg: none` — see ErrUnsignedJWT
135	// for the rationale. The signature payload itself is still not
136	// verified; that remains the issuing server's responsibility.
137	func ParseClaims(jwt string) (*UnverifiedClaims, error) {
138		parts := strings.Split(jwt, ".")
139		if len(parts) != 3 {
140			return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: expected 3 segments, got %d", ErrMalformedJWT, len(parts))
141		}
142	
143		header, err := base64.RawURLEncoding.DecodeString(parts[0])
144		if err != nil {
145			return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: decode header: %w", ErrMalformedJWT, err)
146		}
147		var hdr struct {
148			Alg string `json:"alg"`
149		}
150		if err := json.Unmarshal(header, &hdr); err != nil {
151			return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: parse header: %w", ErrMalformedJWT, err)
152		}
153		// JWS algorithm identifiers (RFC 7515 §4.1.1, IANA "JSON Web
154		// Signature and Encryption Algorithms" registry) are ASCII
155		// alphanumeric only — "HS256", "RS512", "EdDSA", "none", …
156		//
157		// Anything else is malformed. Rejecting non-alphanumeric runes
158		// here closes a class of bypasses against the alg:none check:
159		// `strings.TrimSpace` only handles unicode.IsSpace, missing
160		// U+200B (zero-width space), U+FEFF (BOM), and other invisible
161		// chars that a hostile AS could pad around "none" to slip past
162		// a case-fold comparison.
163		for _, r := range hdr.Alg {
164			if (r >= 'A' && r <= 'Z') || (r >= 'a' && r <= 'z') || (r >= '0' && r <= '9') {
165				continue
166			}
167			return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: alg contains non-alphanumeric character", ErrMalformedJWT)
168		}
169		// Case-insensitive because RFC 7515 §4.1.1 doesn't strictly
170		// canonicalise case, and "None" / "NONE" have been observed in
171		// the wild.
172		if strings.EqualFold(hdr.Alg, "none") {
173			return nil, ErrUnsignedJWT
174		}
175	
176		payload, err := base64.RawURLEncoding.DecodeString(parts[1])
177		if err != nil {
178			return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: decode payload: %w", ErrMalformedJWT, err)
179		}
180	
181		var raw struct {
182			Iss    string          `json:"iss"`
183			Sub    string          `json:"sub"`
184			Aud    json.RawMessage `json:"aud"`
185			Exp    int64           `json:"exp"`
186			Iat    int64           `json:"iat"`
187			Nbf    int64           `json:"nbf"`
188			Handle string          `json:"handle"`
189		}
190		if err := json.Unmarshal(payload, &raw); err != nil {
191			return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: parse payload: %w", ErrMalformedJWT, err)
192		}
193	
194		c := &UnverifiedClaims{
195			Issuer:  raw.Iss,
196			Subject: raw.Sub,
197			Handle:  raw.Handle,
198		}
199	
200		if raw.Exp != 0 {
201			c.ExpiresAt = time.Unix(raw.Exp, 0).UTC()
202		}
203		if raw.Iat != 0 {
204			c.IssuedAt = time.Unix(raw.Iat, 0).UTC()
205		}
206		if raw.Nbf != 0 {
207			c.NotBefore = time.Unix(raw.Nbf, 0).UTC()
208		}
209	
210		c.Audience, err = decodeAudience(raw.Aud)
211		if err != nil {
212			return nil, err
213		}
214	
215		return c, nil
216	}
217	
218	// decodeAudience handles both string and string-array forms of the JWT
219	// `aud` claim.
220	func decodeAudience(raw json.RawMessage) ([]string, error) {
221		if len(raw) == 0 {
222			return nil, nil
223		}
224	
225		var single string
226		if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &single); err == nil {
227			if single == "" {
228				return nil, nil
229			}
230			return []string{single}, nil
231		}
232	
233		var multi []string
234		if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &multi); err == nil {
235			return multi, nil
236		}
237	
238		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: aud claim is neither a string nor a string array", ErrMalformedJWT)
239	}

3	import "time"

5	// MaxExpiresInSeconds caps a server-provided OAuth expires_in (seconds)
6	// before it is multiplied into a time.Duration. Without a ceiling, a value
7	// above ~9.2e9 overflows time.Duration's int64 nanosecond range, wrapping
8	// the derived expiry into the past so a freshly-issued token looks
9	// already-expired. 100 years is far beyond any real token lifetime and
10	// safely below the overflow threshold.
11	const MaxExpiresInSeconds = 100 * 365 * 24 * 60 * 60
12	
13	// ExpiresInDuration converts a server-provided expires_in (seconds) into a
14	// time.Duration, clamping at MaxExpiresInSeconds to avoid int64 overflow.
15	// Callers still gate on expires_in > 0 where a non-positive value is
16	// invalid; this helper only defends the upper bound.
17	func ExpiresInDuration(secs int) time.Duration {
18		if secs > MaxExpiresInSeconds {
19			secs = MaxExpiresInSeconds
20		}
21		return time.Duration(secs) * time.Second
22	}

5	// HTTPClient builds the *http.Client used for one OAuth request.
6	//
7	// Always returns a freshly-allocated *http.Client so this library's
8	// requests are isolated from mutations to http.DefaultClient (any
9	// process-wide Timeout or Transport swap by another package would
10	// otherwise be inherited). The underlying Transport is the
11	// caller-supplied transport when non-nil, or http.DefaultTransport
12	// otherwise — sharing a Transport is intentional (it owns the
13	// connection pool) and safe (Transport.RoundTrip is concurrent-safe).
14	//
15	// Per-request timeouts must be driven by ctx.WithTimeout in the
16	// caller, not by *http.Client.Timeout — the body-read happens after
17	// client.Do returns, and Client.Timeout would cancel that read.
18	func HTTPClient(transport http.RoundTripper) *http.Client {
19		if transport == nil {
20			transport = http.DefaultTransport
21		}
22		return &http.Client{Transport: transport}
23	}

1	package oauthhttp
2	
3	import "strings"
4	
5	// MaxErrorDescriptionRunes caps a sanitised server-supplied
6	// error_description by rune count. Real values are short ("user
7	// denied", "code expired", "audience denied"); past this the
8	// truncated form points at server misbehaviour rather than
9	// user-facing guidance, and unbounded length is a UX-DoS vector.
10	// Counted in runes rather than bytes so truncation lands on a valid
11	// UTF-8 boundary.
12	const MaxErrorDescriptionRunes = 512
13	
14	// SanitizeDescription strips control characters and caps length so
15	// a hostile or buggy AS can't write into the user's terminal or
16	// balloon CLI logs via the error_description field of an OAuth error
17	// response.
18	//
19	// Rejected ranges:
20	//
21	//   - C0 controls (U+0000–U+001F): ESC (0x1b) for ANSI sequences,
22	//     CR, LF, TAB, NUL, BEL, etc.
23	//   - DEL (U+007F).
24	//   - C1 controls (U+0080–U+009F): notably CSI (U+009B), which is
25	//     functionally equivalent to "ESC [" in 8-bit-aware terminals
26	//     and can start an ANSI escape sequence on its own.
27	//
28	// Preserves printable Unicode (including non-ASCII); truncates on
29	// rune boundaries rather than byte offsets so a CJK / emoji /
30	// combining-character payload can't be cut mid-rune into invalid
31	// UTF-8.
32	func SanitizeDescription(s string) string {
33		if s == "" {
34			return ""
35		}
36		var b strings.Builder
37		b.Grow(len(s))
38		runes := 0
39		truncated := false
40		for _, r := range s {
41			switch {
42			case r < 0x20: // C0 controls
43				continue
44			case r == 0x7f: // DEL
45				continue
46			case r >= 0x80 && r <= 0x9f: // C1 controls (includes CSI U+009B)
47				continue
48			}
49			if runes >= MaxErrorDescriptionRunes {
50				truncated = true
51				break
52			}
53			b.WriteRune(r)
54			runes++
55		}
56		out := strings.TrimSpace(b.String())
57		if truncated {
58			out += "…"
59		}
60		return out
61	}

# Changelog

## Unreleased

### Changed

- Bumped the Go toolchain (and the `go.mod` minimum) to 1.26.4, picking
  up the standard-library security fixes GO-2026-5037 (`crypto/x509`
  hostname parsing) and GO-2026-5039 (`net/textproto`). Consumers now
  require Go ≥ 1.26.4.

### Added

- `sts.ExchangeError` — a typed error returned by `Client.Exchange` when
  the token endpoint replies with a structured RFC 6749 OAuth error.
  Exposes the parsed `Code`, `Description`, and `StatusCode` so callers
  can branch on the failure mode (e.g. `errors.As` + `Code ==
  "invalid_target"`) instead of substring-matching the message. `Error()`
  renders the same string as before, so message-matching callers are
  unaffected; non-OAuth failures (network errors, non-JSON bodies) remain
  plain wrapped errors.

## v0.4.0 — 2026-05-28

### Added

- New `refresh` package: an RFC 6749 §6 `refresh_token` grant client
  (peer of `sts`/`deviceflow`) that re-mints the login JWT from a stored
  refresh token. Exposes `refresh.ErrInvalidGrant` for rotation-race
  handling.
- `tokenmanager.Token` now transparently re-mints an expired/near-expiry
  login JWT from the stored refresh token before resolving the request,
  re-prompting login only when the refresh token itself is revoked or
  expired. New exported `tokenmanager.Manager.Refresh` lets callers warm
  the session proactively.
- Cross-process single-flight for refresh: an in-process mutex plus an
  injectable `tokenmanager.ProcessLock` (default: an advisory file lock
  over `golang.org/x/sys`), with rotation-race tolerance (on
  `invalid_grant`, the store is re-read and the refresh retried once

# auth-go — shareable OAuth 2.0 client library for CLIs

[![Tests](https://github.com/entireio/auth-go/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/entireio/auth-go/actions/workflows/test.yml)
[![Lint](https://github.com/entireio/auth-go/actions/workflows/lint.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/entireio/auth-go/actions/workflows/lint.yml)
[![Go Reference](https://pkg.go.dev/badge/github.com/entireio/auth-go.svg)](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/entireio/auth-go)

Provider-agnostic Go library for CLIs that authenticate end-users via OAuth 2.0 device flow (RFC 8628), present resource-scoped bearer tokens to data APIs, and (when the auth host and data API live on different origins) exchange tokens via RFC 8693 STS.

No global state, no env-var reads, no implicit URLs. Every endpoint, identifier, and default value is supplied by the embedding CLI through a `Config` struct.

```
go get github.com/entireio/auth-go@latest
```

## Subpackages

| Package | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`deviceflow`](./deviceflow/) | RFC 8628 OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant client. Polls the token endpoint, surfaces RFC 8628 §3.5 error codes (`authorization_pending`, `slow_down`, `access_denied`, `expired_token`, `invalid_grant`) as Go sentinels with optional `error_description`. |
| [`sts`](./sts/) | RFC 8693 OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange client. Provider-agnostic — caller supplies endpoint path, `subject_token_type`, `requested_token_type`, optional `audience` / `resource` / `scope`, and any provider-specific `Extra` form fields (e.g. `client_id`). |
| [`tokens`](./tokens/) | `TokenSet` value type plus unverified JWT claim parsing. Rejects `alg:none` (RFC 7515 / RFC 7518 §3.6 known attack vector). The package never validates signatures — that's the issuing server's responsibility. Callers use `Claims` for routing decisions (which issuer, which audience) and UX (display the principal handle), not as a security boundary. |
| [`tokenstore`](./tokenstore/) | `Store` interface for token persistence + `Keyring` reference impl backed by `github.com/zalando/go-keyring`. Each CLI passes its own service name so credentials are isolated across CLIs sharing this library. Returns `ErrNotFound` for unknown profiles and `ErrMalformed` (wrapped) when a stored entry exists but can't be decoded — used by upgrade fallbacks. |
| [`tokenmanager`](./tokenmanager/) | Orchestration: stores the device-flow core token, runs RFC 8693 exchanges when needed to obtain resource-scoped bearers, caches the results until expiry, and short-circuits when no exchange is needed (same-host or core-token's `aud` already covers the resource). Most CLIs only need to interact with this package directly. |

The `internal/oauthhttp` package holds shared HTTP body-reading + JSON-decoding helpers (detects HTML responses from captive portals / proxy intercepts and surfaces them as actionable errors instead of unmarshal failures). It is unexported in the Go sense — not importable by other modules — and not part of the public API surface.

## Security

Defense-in-depth checks layered on top of server-side validation:

- **HTTPS required.** Both `sts.Client` and `deviceflow.Client` reject `http://` BaseURLs unless `AllowInsecureHTTP` is set, and that opt-in is still limited to loopback (`localhost` / `127.0.0.1` / `::1`) so production misconfigurations fail loudly.
- **`alg:none` JWTs rejected.** `tokens.ParseClaims` decodes the JWT header and refuses the unsigned shape (any case variant of `none`). Even though claim use is routing-only, this keeps an obvious attack surface closed.
- **`verification_uri` validated.** The device-code response field is what your CLI echoes and opens in the user's browser — a malicious AS pointing it at a phishing page would be a credential-harvesting vector. The library rejects non-https (loopback http excepted), embedded `user:pass@host` userinfo, and control characters in the URI.
- **Resource origins validated.** `tokenmanager.Token` requires `TokenRequest.Resource` to be an origin URL: absolute scheme + host, HTTPS unless loopback HTTP is explicitly enabled, and no userinfo/path/query/fragment. This prevents cache fragmentation and accidental STS requests for surprising resource strings.
- **OAuth responses are bounded and strict.** Success and error bodies are capped at `MaxResponseBytes`; oversized responses are rejected, HTML/captive-portal responses get actionable errors, and JSON success bodies with trailing data are refused.
- **STS wire shape is explicit.** `tokenmanager` defaults `subject_token_type` to the RFC 8693 access-token URN and exposes `Config.SubjectTokenType` for STS endpoints that require the structural JWT URN.

# Changelog

## Unreleased

### Changed

- Bumped the Go toolchain (and the `go.mod` minimum) to 1.26.4, picking
  up the standard-library security fixes GO-2026-5037 (`crypto/x509`
  hostname parsing) and GO-2026-5039 (`net/textproto`). Consumers now
  require Go ≥ 1.26.4.

### Added

- `sts.ExchangeError` — a typed error returned by `Client.Exchange` when
  the token endpoint replies with a structured RFC 6749 OAuth error.
  Exposes the parsed `Code`, `Description`, and `StatusCode` so callers
  can branch on the failure mode (e.g. `errors.As` + `Code ==
  "invalid_target"`) instead of substring-matching the message. `Error()`
  renders the same string as before, so message-matching callers are
  unaffected; non-OAuth failures (network errors, non-JSON bodies) remain
  plain wrapped errors.

## v0.4.0 — 2026-05-28

### Added

- New `refresh` package: an RFC 6749 §6 `refresh_token` grant client
  (peer of `sts`/`deviceflow`) that re-mints the login JWT from a stored
  refresh token. Exposes `refresh.ErrInvalidGrant` for rotation-race
  handling.
- `tokenmanager.Token` now transparently re-mints an expired/near-expiry
  login JWT from the stored refresh token before resolving the request,
  re-prompting login only when the refresh token itself is revoked or
  expired. New exported `tokenmanager.Manager.Refresh` lets callers warm
  the session proactively.
- Cross-process single-flight for refresh: an in-process mutex plus an
  injectable `tokenmanager.ProcessLock` (default: an advisory file lock
  over `golang.org/x/sys`), with rotation-race tolerance (on
  `invalid_grant`, the store is re-read and the refresh retried once
  against a concurrently-rotated successor before concluding re-login).
- New `tokenmanager.Config` fields `RefreshPath` (token endpoint for the
  refresh grant) and `LockDir` (advisory-lock directory; defaults under
  `os.UserCacheDir()`).
- New sentinels `tokenmanager.ErrReauthRequired` (refresh exhausted —
  distinct from `ErrNotLoggedIn`) and `tokenmanager.ErrNoRefreshPath`.

### Changed

- `golang.org/x/sys` is now a direct dependency (advisory file lock).
- `client_id` validation (`ValidateClientID` / `ValidateClientIDConsistency`)
  moved into `internal/oauthhttp` and shared by `sts` and `refresh`; no
  behavioural change to `sts`.
- Clamp a server-provided `expires_in` before converting to a
  `time.Duration` (centralised in `internal/oauthhttp.ExpiresInDuration`),
  applied across `sts`, `deviceflow`, and `refresh`. Guards against an
  int64 nanosecond overflow that an absurd value would otherwise wrap into
  a past expiry.
- `tokenmanager.SaveCoreToken` and `tokenmanager.DeleteCoreToken` now
  acquire the refresh lock (`refreshMu` in-process, the cross-process file
  lock) before mutating the store, serialising them against in-flight
  refreshes. Prevents a refresh whose grant is mid-flight from persisting
  over a concurrent logout (session resurrection) or overwriting a
  concurrent re-login. Both methods can now block up to ~30s under
  contention and may return a wrapped lock-acquire error.

## v0.3.4 — 2026-05-25

### Breaking changes

- `tokenmanager.Token` now requires `TokenRequest.Resource` to be an origin URL: absolute scheme + host, HTTPS unless loopback HTTP is explicitly enabled, and no userinfo/path/query/fragment. Opaque or non-URL resource strings that previously flowed through byte-exact are now rejected; use `Audience` for opaque audience values and `Resource` for the API origin.
- `tokenmanager.New` now holds `Config.Issuer` to the same origin-URL contract as `TokenRequest.Resource`. Issuers carrying userinfo, a path, query, or fragment are rejected at construction. Previously they were accepted and silently mis-fired the same-host shortcut, forcing every "same origin" call through the STS.
- `sts.Client.Exchange` now rejects multi-valued `Extra["client_id"]`. Different server-side form parsers picked different entries, so the wire identity was caller-invisible.

### Security

- Sanitise the AS-supplied OAuth `error` code before interpolating it into returned errors. The description was already sanitised; the code field was a parallel terminal-escape sink.
- `validateVerificationURI` rejects C1 controls (U+0080–U+009F) in addition to C0 + DEL. CSI (U+009B) is the canonical 8-bit-aware terminal-escape bypass.
- Hardened OAuth response parsing and sanitization, including oversized response rejection, trailing JSON rejection, and sanitized fallback text for non-JSON error bodies.
- Centralised OAuth HTTP helpers in `internal/oauthhttp` (origin-URL normalisation/validation, OAuth error parsing, response decoding, sanitisation) to eliminate per-package drift.
- Restricted explicit insecure HTTP opt-in to loopback hosts.
- Added `govulncheck` to the mise lint task and CI workflow.

cd /Users/paul/src/entireio/auth-go && git commit -F - <<'EOF'
authcode: add RFC 8252 loopback authorization-code + PKCE client

New `authcode` package: a sibling to `deviceflow` implementing the
RFC 8252 native-app loopback flow with PKCE (RFC 7636, S256).

- `Client.Start` binds a 127.0.0.1 listener, computes the PKCE
  verifier + state, and returns a `Flow` carrying the browser
  `AuthorizationURL`.
- `Flow.Wait` blocks for the loopback redirect and returns the
  authorization code (rejecting state-mismatched/forged callbacks
  without aborting the pending login).
- `Flow.Exchange` redeems the code + verifier at the token endpoint
  for a `tokens.TokenSet`.

Opening the browser stays the caller's responsibility, matching
`deviceflow`. Reuses `internal/oauthhttp` for URL resolution, JSON
decode, OAuth-error parsing, description sanitization, and expiry
clamping, so the captive-portal/size-cap/loopback hardening applies
here too. Sentinels: ErrAccessDenied, ErrInvalidGrant, ErrMissingCode,
ErrListenerClosed; re-exports ErrInsecureBaseURL / ErrAbsolutePath.

Docs: new subpackage row in README, doc.go umbrella entry, CHANGELOG
Added entry, and removed the now-stale "PKCE is a non-goal" line.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

input.content:
## What

New `authcode` package — a sibling to `deviceflow` — implementing the RFC 8252 native-app **loopback authorization-code flow with PKCE** (RFC 7636, S256).

- `Client.Start` binds a `127.0.0.1` listener, computes the PKCE verifier + state, and returns a `Flow` with the browser `AuthorizationURL`.
- `Flow.Wait` blocks for the loopback redirect and returns the authorization code (state-mismatched/forged callbacks are rejected without aborting the pending login).
- `Flow.Exchange` redeems the code + verifier at the token endpoint for a `tokens.TokenSet`.

Opening the browser stays the caller's responsibility, matching `deviceflow`. Reuses `internal/oauthhttp` for URL resolution, JSON decode, OAuth-error parsing, description sanitization, and expiry clamping — so the captive-portal / size-cap / loopback hardening applies here too. Sentinels: `ErrAccessDenied`, `ErrInvalidGrant`, `ErrMissingCode`, `ErrListenerClosed`; re-exports `ErrInsecureBaseURL` / `ErrAbsolutePath`.

## Why now (it wasn't here before)

The library shipped device-flow-only on purpose — and for headless/CI that's still the right default. But we want the smoothest UX where it's available:

- On a **local, interactive machine with a browser**, loopback code flow is genuinely nicer: nothing to type, no polling latency.
- Mature CLIs (`gh`, `gcloud`, `aws sso`) ship **both** and fall back to device flow when there's no usable browser/localhost.

This PR adds the building block so the CLI can default to the browser flow interactively and fall back to device flow otherwise. (CLI wiring is a follow-up PR.)

## Tests

12 table/unit tests covering the happy path (incl. end-to-end PKCE verifier↔challenge check), authorize-URL construction, scope omission, state-mismatch tolerance, access-denied, missing-code, wait timeout, context cancellation, invalid_grant, missing-token, `New` validation, and insecure-BaseURL rejection. All pass under `-race`.

> Note: lint not run locally (offline); relying on CI.

## What

`entire login` now defaults to the **loopback authorization-code flow** (browser): open a browser, get redirected to a local `127.0.0.1` listener, exchange the code for tokens. No code to copy, no poll latency.

The **device-code flow** stays available behind `--device`, and is the **automatic fallback** when there's no interactive terminal (CI, piped, SSH without a tty).

```
entire login            # browser flow (interactive); device flow if headless
entire login --device   # force the device-code flow
```

## Why (it wasn't built this way originally)

Device-flow-only was a deliberate starting point, and it's still the right default for headless/CI. But we want the smoothest UX where it's available:

- On a **local, interactive machine with a browser**, loopback code flow is genuinely nicer — nothing to type, no polling latency.
- Mature CLIs (`gh`, `gcloud`, `aws sso`) ship **both** and fall back to device flow when there's no usable browser/localhost. This PR mirrors that shape.

## Changes

- **provider**: add `AuthorizePath` (v1 `/oauth/authorize`, v2 `/authorize`).
- **auth.Client**: build an `authcode.Client` alongside the deviceflow client; expose `StartBrowserAuth` + a `BrowserAuthFlow` shim (parallel to the existing deviceflow shim), flattening `TokenSet` → `(access, refresh)`.
- **login.go**: `shouldUseBrowserLogin()` flow selection, `runBrowserLogin()`, and a shared `persistLogin()` tail reused by both flows. `openBrowser` is a no-op under test so the browser flow is testable without launching a real browser.

## Tests

- Unit: flow-selector table + `runBrowserLogin` error/messaging paths.
- Integration: full loopback flow driven by playing the browser (GET the callback with the `state` parsed off the printed authorize URL).
- Existing device-flow tests now exercise the `--device` / non-interactive fallback path.

## ⚠️ Before merge (stacked PR)

1. **Stacked on** entireio/auth-go's `authcode` package PR — merge + tag that first, then bump here: `go get github.com/entireio/auth-go@<tag> && go mod tidy`. Until then this branch does not build (the `authcode` import is unresolved).
2. **Confirm the v2 `AuthorizePath`** (`/authorize`) against the auth host's `/.well-known/openid-configuration` `authorization_endpoint`, and confirm `entire-cli` is registered as a public client with a loopback redirect (`http://127.0.0.1/callback`, any port).

## What

`entire login` now defaults to the **loopback authorization-code flow** (browser): open a browser, get redirected to a local `127.0.0.1` listener, exchange the code for tokens. No code to copy, no poll latency.

The **device-code flow** stays available behind `--device`, and is the **automatic fallback** when there's no interactive terminal (CI, piped, SSH without a tty).

- On a **local, interactive machine with a browser**, loopback code flow is genuinely nicer — nothing to type, no polling latency.

input.command:
git add cmd/entire/cli/login.go cmd/entire/cli/login_test.go cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/login_test.go && git status -sb && git commit -F - <<'EOF'
login: show auth host instead of the long authorize URL

The browser flow now prints "Logging in to:  <auth host>" rather than
the full authorize URL (the PKCE challenge + loopback redirect made it
long and unreadable). The full URL is shown only as a fallback when the
browser can't be opened, which is also what a headless host hits.

openBrowser reports failure under test (no usable browser on a CI host,
and we mustn't spawn a real one), so the integration test recovers the
ephemeral loopback callback URL from that fallback line on stdout —
replacing the file-based seam from the previous iteration.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
